series.name: The Wedding Planner
series.tagline: She's planned 200 weddings. She knows which ones will last.
series.concept: Naina Khurana — 38, runs a boutique wedding planning firm in Delhi. Each episode: one couple obsessing over the wrong detail, one Daniel Gilbert concept about why we are spectacularly bad at predicting what will make us happy. The expensive venue, not the guest list. The perfect dress, not the right partner. The flash-mob choreography, not the mother-in-law.

episodes.title: The Sangeet Choreographer

slides.text:
Aanya, 28. Karan, 30.

Wedding in four months.
Jaipur palace. 600 guests.
Budget: ₹2.4 crore.

The planner — me — has been hired in October.
The wedding is in February.

We have one hundred and twenty days.

My clipboard says: Day 1, sangeet rehearsal.

Day 7.

Aanya is in a banquet hall in Defence Colony.

She is fighting with the choreographer.

It is the third version of the flash-mob.

She wants Karan's six college friends to enter from the back
at the chorus drop
and do the bridge in slow motion.

They have known the bride for seven days.

They live in three different cities.

What Aanya has not done in the same week:

— spoken to Karan's mother for more than 11 minutes
— asked where the mother will sleep after the wedding
— asked whether the mother eats onions
— asked the mother anything

The mother is moving in.

The sangeet is one night.

The mother is the rest of her life.

From my notebook, Day 7:

"They are fighting about the dance.

They are not fighting about the woman who will be in the kitchen on the third Sunday of every month for the next thirty years.

They are optimizing for the wrong day."

THE FOCUSING ILLUSION

Gilbert: "Nothing in life is as important as you think it is when you are thinking about it."

When you are rehearsing a sangeet,
the sangeet feels like the most important thing in your life.

It isn't.

It's the dinner table.
It's the third Sunday.
It's the woman in the kitchen.

I do not lecture brides.

I do one small thing.

I call Karan's mother.

I say: "Auntie ji, Aanya wants you to come bless the dance rehearsal tomorrow."

Aanya didn't say that.

Auntie ji says yes immediately.

Day 8. Rehearsal.

Auntie ji arrives. Sits on a folding chair.

The music starts.

Aanya dances. The flash-mob enters. The bridge happens in slow motion.

Auntie ji says one sentence after, kindly:

"Beta, your hand was a little stiff in the second part."

Aanya does not sleep that night.

Not because of the dance.

Next time on The Wedding Planner:

A bride spends ₹8 lakhs on a Sabyasachi lehenga.

Six months after the wedding, she will not take it out of the box.

The dress is doing exactly what dresses do.

The dress is not the problem.

Episode 2: The Lehenga.

episodes.synopsis: Aanya (28) and Karan (30), Punjabi-Sindhi match, wedding in four months at a Jaipur palace. Aanya has been at war with the choreographer for a week about a flash-mob she wants Karan's college friends to learn for the sangeet. She has not, in the same week, had a single conversation with Karan's mother that lasted more than 11 minutes. The mother is moving in after the wedding. Naina watches the rehearsal and decides to do the one thing the bride does not want — she invites the mother to bless the dance.
episodes.caption:
Aanya fought for a week with the choreographer about a flash-mob.

In the same week, she had not had a single conversation with Karan's mother that lasted more than 11 minutes. The mother is moving in.

Daniel Gilbert calls this the focusing illusion: nothing in life is as important as you think it is when you are thinking about it.

The sangeet is one night. The mother is the rest of your life.

What did you optimize for at your wedding — or the one you're planning?

episodes.title: The Lehenga
episodes.synopsis: Pari (27) buys a ₹8 lakh Sabyasachi for her Jaipur wedding. The first try-on, she cries. The wedding day, she glows. Six months later, the lehenga is in a box on top of her wardrobe. Naina, who has watched 200 brides do this, names what is happening: the dress is doing exactly what dresses do. The thrill of any acquired thing has a half-life. The brain that gives you the high is the same brain that, by design, takes it away — so it can remain interested in the next thing. The dress is not the problem. The forecast was.

episodes.title: The Guest List
episodes.synopsis: He wants 800 guests. She wants 80. Three weeks of fighting. Naina watches them and realizes the fight is not about logistics or budget. It is about whose family will register as the bigger family on the day. Comparison is the silent thief of every Indian wedding — bride compares to her cousin's reception, groom compares to his college roommate's destination wedding, both families compare guest counts as proxy for love. Gilbert: a dollar in your pocket feels different depending on how many dollars are in your neighbour's. So does a guest.

episodes.title: The Venue Tour
episodes.synopsis: The bride wants a fifth visit to the Udaipur venue. She is imagining the wedding — sunset over the lake, mandap on the water, fairy lights, the moment. She is not imagining what it will feel like to be married to him on a Tuesday in November when the maid is on leave and the AC is broken. Gilbert: imagination paints in the parts you ask it about, and leaves the rest blank. The blank parts are most of the marriage.

episodes.title: The Photographer
episodes.synopsis: ₹6 lakh for a celebrity photographer. The album arrives three months later. They look at it twice. The wedding-day photos go up on Instagram and stay frozen there. Naina names the trade: a thousand mundane Tuesdays of small joy will produce more total happiness than one curated Saturday. We optimize for the curated Saturday because it is photographable. The Tuesdays are not. The brain is a poor accountant of the unphotographed.

episodes.title: The Date Fight
episodes.synopsis: The astrologer says June. They want October. Two weeks of fighting. The October feeling they are arguing about — that fairytale autumn-Delhi-light feeling — is not the October feeling that will arrive when October arrives. By then they will be eight months married. Tired. Possibly happier in a less photogenic way. Gilbert: every prediction we make about future feelings is contaminated by the temperature of the present. The present is a poor sample.

episodes.title: The Vegan Menu
episodes.synopsis: The bride insists on a fully vegan menu because a friend's wedding had one and 'it was so different, so special, so them.' Naina has done this menu twice before. It was not, statistically, more memorable than the buffet. Specialness is not a function of the menu — it is a function of who you have at the table. The bride has been told this. She knows it. She will do the menu anyway, because Gilbert's most universal bias is believing that the rules of human happiness apply to other people, not to her wedding.

episodes.title: The Pre-Wedding Shoot
episodes.synopsis: Three days. Three cities. Udaipur for the heritage shot, Goa for the breeze, Mumbai for the skyline. The couple believes the variety will produce a richer memory. It will produce roughly the same memory as one good afternoon in any of the three. Gilbert: variety boosts pleasure when the episodes are close together — chocolate, then strawberry, then vanilla in one sitting. When the episodes are spaced out, sameness is fine, because the gap resets the palate. The pre-wedding shoot is the gap of three months. They are buying variety they will not actually taste.

episodes.title: The Honeymoon
episodes.synopsis: ₹14 lakh on the honeymoon. They have not, in the entire planning, had a single conversation about money. They will, in March, when the credit card bill arrives and they realize they have different definitions of a 'reasonable' EMI. Gilbert: the future feels far away because it is, neurologically, encoded as someone else. We are kind to ourselves now and rude to that other person, who turns out, embarrassingly, to also be us.

episodes.title: The Eleventh Fitting
episodes.synopsis: The bride hates her lehenga at the eleventh fitting. The same lehenga she chose, with no coercion, six months ago. She will love it on the wedding day. She will hate it again at the first anniversary. She will love it at the tenth, when she shows it to her daughter. Gilbert: once we choose, the brain quietly works to make us right about the choice. Until something resets the comparison. Then it works again.

episodes.title: The Right Boy
episodes.synopsis: Arranged match. The bride sits in Naina's office for what is supposed to be a venue discussion. Five minutes in, she asks the question she has been carrying for months. 'Naina, you've seen so many couples. Will I be happy?' Naina almost answers honestly. Then she gives the planner answer. The truth, which Gilbert would say: the data show people adapt either way. The people who marry their college sweetheart and the people who marry the second cousin their aunt suggested report similar happiness levels at year five. The data also do not tell you whether to want what you would adapt to.

episodes.title: The Outdoor Mandap
episodes.synopsis: She wants the mandap outdoors. December in Delhi. Imagined version: candles, breeze, fairy lights, magazine photo. Actual version: 6°C, two pashminas under the lehenga, the priest visibly shivering, the groom unable to feel his fingers for the rings. Gilbert: imagination is a screenwriter, not a meteorologist. It writes the scene and leaves out the weather. The weather always arrives anyway.

episodes.title: The DJ
episodes.synopsis: A month-long fight about which DJ to book. Two days after the wedding, the bride will not remember which one they hired. While they are deciding, it feels — bodily, viscerally — like the most important question in their lives. Gilbert: the foreground swallows the frame. This is not weakness. This is how the brain is built. The work is to remember that everything currently in your foreground will, predictably, recede.

episodes.title: The First Anniversary
episodes.synopsis: A couple comes back to Naina's office to plan their first anniversary celebration. The wedding had been, by all accounts, perfect. The marriage isn't. They are not unhappy. They are confused — they did everything right, and the everyday is harder than they imagined. Naina realizes the most expensive forecasting error of all: treating one Saturday as a prediction of 18,000 ordinary days. The wedding measures the wedding. It does not measure what comes after. We keep using it as a proxy anyway.

episodes.title: The Ex on the Guest List
episodes.synopsis: The bride's ex-boyfriend is on her family's invite list because his mother and her mother are college friends. She is destroyed for two months. Cannot sleep, cannot focus on the planning. On the day, she sees him for thirty seconds, says hello, walks past, forgets him by the second course. Gilbert: the body comes equipped with an immune system for adversity that is louder than we credit. The fear of a thing is almost always more painful than the thing.

episodes.title: The Empty Chair
episodes.synopsis: The bride's father has refused to come to the wedding because of an old caste-related family feud. She is destroyed for three weeks. Cannot eat, cannot pick the menu, cannot finalize the music. On the wedding morning she dresses, eats two boiled eggs, walks to the mandap, and barely thinks of him. Months later, she will say it was the most beautiful day of her life. Both things are true. Adaptation is not betrayal. Adaptation is what allows us to keep living.

episodes.title: The Cancelled Wedding
episodes.synopsis: Three days before the wedding. The bride calls it off. Her family is in agony. The vendors have to be paid anyway. Six months later she meets Naina for chai and says, with evident peace, that it was the best decision of her life. She believes it. Gilbert: she is right to. The brain that we use to feel good about chosen outcomes is the same brain we use to feel good about the outcomes we wanted. There is no second-class happiness. There is only happiness.

episodes.title: The Diet
episodes.synopsis: Twelve kilos lost in eight months for the wedding fitting. Twelve kilos back in six months after. The bride is shocked. Naina is not. Every bride thinks the lehenga-fitting body is the body forever. None of them are. Gilbert: we are aware that we have changed enormously over the past ten years. We are convinced we will not change much over the next ten. This is one of the most reliably wrong predictions humans make.

episodes.title: The Mother-in-Law
episodes.synopsis: Bride and mother-in-law are at war for the entire wedding planning. Two years later, the MIL is the only one who comes to the hospital when the bride is admitted with dengue. Naina runs into them at INA market a year after that, holding hands. The current version of any relationship is the version we use to forecast all future versions. The forecast is almost always wrong, in either direction. People become other people. Sometimes that is the whole story of a marriage.

episodes.title: The Seventh Pheri
episodes.synopsis: Couple at the mandap, doing the seven steps. Sanskrit vows about loyalty, prosperity, children, lifelong companionship. Beautiful. Ancient. Forecast-rich. None of which they have any honest instrument to predict. Gilbert would not say don't make the vows. He would say: notice that the vow is a forecast made by a self that will not exist by the time the vow needs to be kept. The keeping is not done by today's self. It is done, daily, by future selves who will have to choose.

episodes.title: The Same Lehenga
episodes.synopsis: Two cousins. Same lehenga design, six months apart. The first bride is delighted with hers. The second bride, having seen her cousin's photos before her own wedding, finds her version unbearable. Same dress. Same vendor. Same budget. Different reference point. Different feeling. Naina has stopped showing brides their friends' wedding photos for this exact reason. The reference point is the experience.

episodes.title: The Influencer Wedding
episodes.synopsis: The bride is a small lifestyle creator with 80,000 followers. Every detail of the wedding is posted in real time. She spends her own sangeet checking the engagement on her stories. The wedding is happening to the followers, with her present. Naina watches and wonders, mid-event, whether the bride will remember anything that wasn't rehearsed for the camera. Gilbert: the act of curating an experience for an audience changes what the experience is. We are increasingly the audience to our own lives.

episodes.title: The Couple Who Eloped
episodes.synopsis: A couple who skipped the whole production. Court marriage, two witnesses, samosa-and-chai with parents at home. They contact Naina five years later for a vow renewal — which they then also cancel. They describe the original day like a film. Their friends, who spent ₹2 crore on a Jaisalmer wedding the same year, do not. Memory is a writer with revisions, not a camera. The smaller the original footage, the more freedom the writer has.

episodes.title: The Repeat Bride
episodes.synopsis: Same client. Second wedding. She cannot remember why the first one was unbearable. Naina has, somewhere in her phone, the WhatsApp chats from 2018 to prove the bride once said she would never marry again. The brain is kind in this way. The brain is also a liar in this way. Gilbert: the function of forgetting bad pain is to permit good action. Without it, no one would have a second child, a second business, or a second wedding.

episodes.title: The Planner's Question
episodes.synopsis: Naina, 38. Has planned 200 weddings. Is, statistically, the most informed unmarried person in Delhi about whether weddings work. Gilbert's prescription is clear: surrogate. Ask people who have lived a life like the one you're imagining. Trust their report. Naina has done that 200 times. She still hasn't decided. The series ends with her closing her notebook on a Friday evening, looking at one wedding photograph on her wall — not hers — and naming the limit of every science of happiness ever written. The science can describe what will probably make you feel good. It cannot tell you whether to want to feel good in that particular way. Some things, including marriage, are not happiness optimizations. They are commitments. The teacher does not, this time, do the homework. She gets up. She turns off the light. She locks the office. She walks down to her car.
